title: Birth of Stars: Nebulae and Protostars

cards.h: Stars are being born right now
cards.b: Stars live for millions to trillions of years, so we cannot watch one grow. But the sky holds stars of every age at once, like a forest with seedlings and old trees. In the Milky Way about one to two new Sun-like stars form each year, in dark, cold clouds.

Stars form in molecular clouds: cold (about 10 K), dense clouds of hydrogen gas (as H2 molecules) and dust, weighing thousands to millions of Suns. Dust blocks starlight, so they look like black patches, e.g. the Horsehead Nebula. In them the gas is cold enough that gravity can beat the pressure.

A part of the cloud, nudged by a shockwave from a nearby supernova, a collision of clouds or a passing spiral arm, becomes dense enough that gravity wins. This is the Jeans instability. The clump falls inward and fragments into many cores, which is why stars are born in clusters, like the Pleiades.

Collapsing material heats up. A hot, glowing, not-yet-fusing core forms: a protostar. Spin flattens the surrounding material into a disc and it also launches two jets along the axis, which carry away spin. The disc feeds the star and later forms planets, as in lesson 1-0-4.

When the core reaches about 10 million K, hydrogen fusion starts and the star joins the main sequence. If the object is lighter than about 0.08 Suns (80 Jupiters), the core never gets hot enough for hydrogen fusion; it becomes a brown dwarf. At the top, stars above roughly 100 Suns are rare because radiation tears them up. Small stars are much more common than large ones.

Newborn massive stars blow winds and ionising light that carve cavities and may stop further star formation, or compress neighbouring gas and trigger it. The famous Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula (Hubble 1995, JWST 2022) are towers of gas being eroded by such stars.

Visible light cannot pass through dense dust, but infrared and radio can. The Orion Nebula, about 1,350 light-years away and visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy 'star' in Orion's sword, holds stars at all ages. Spitzer, Herschel, ALMA and JWST reveal protostars, discs and jets, matching the theory.

• 'Nebulae are just pretty clouds.' They are both nurseries and graveyards.
  • 'A star forms in one go.' Formation takes up to a few million years.
  • 'Brown dwarfs are planets.' They are heavier than planets but too light to be true stars.

In Indian tradition Orion is Mriga, the deer, with Mrigashira a nakshatra; the three stars of Orion's belt were seen as an arrow aimed at it. The GMRT maps cold hydrogen gas through the 21 cm radio line, tracing the gas that forms stars. ISRO's AstroSat Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope has studied young hot stars in star clusters and galaxies.

• Stars form from cold, dense molecular clouds that collapse under gravity.
  • A protostar with a disc and jets forms first; fusion starts at about 10 million K.
  • Below 0.08 solar masses, an object is a brown dwarf.
  • Infrared and radio let us see inside nurseries like Orion.

Think about it: (1) Why are stars often born in groups? (2) Why do hot young stars end up destroying their own nursery?
